searchText: Finding peers in Ethereum would always be hard. But there's a particularly large amount of rigmarole in getting basic blockchain data. I don't think it's just about needing to git gud. For someone who just wants to check out transactions for basic fees/block sizes, and get the last 2 weeks of blocks, it almost seems easier to just outright scrape etherscan or something. I've heard I need ~ 1 TB SSDs, and take days/weeks to download, or use "light mode" geth, which struggles to find peers. dECEntRAlizATIoN That feels like you don't have inbound ports open, like you are behind a nat. or you turned off dns discovery. This is a good guess and I will check. However, when I googled this, there is evidence that "light mode" service is structurally poorly provisioned. I do not know enough to make a normative judgement on whether this is relevant. It is an "experimental" feature. https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/80255/run-geth-light-mode-looking-for-peers-forever https://www.reddit.com/r/ethereum/comments/gb94o1/waiting_for_geth_light_peers_be_like/ https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/10287/ethereum-wallet-is-looking-for-peers-with-geth-light Alright, it took me almost an entire hour but I got the ETH block data. Steps so others do not need to endure this sufferfest: 1. Download and run this geth node thingy https://geth.ethereum.org/downloads/ Once this is installed, you have to run Geth at the command line. You'll wantt to use some special commands: light mode (so you don't have to download the whole blockchain thingy), RPC port, and a large cache helps. `geth --rpc --rpcapi eth,net,web3,personal --cache=4420 --syncmode light --rpcport 8545 --rpcaddr 127.0.0.1 --rpccorsdomain "*"` 2. Download this actually excellent Python package (has a few regular Python dependency jankiness) https://github.com/blockchain-etl/ethereum-etl Run this command to use ethereum-etl `ethereumetl export_blocks_and_transactions --start-block 11967245 --end-block 11967745 --blocks-output blocks.csv --transactions-output transactions.csv --provider-uri http://localhost:8545/ ` Now you're back to actual civilization with a CSV. <@!281951730353045508> Not sure if you are still interested in this project. Just in case it's relevant, here's an abridged sample of the output, in relational data form (if you need this cleaned up or processed let me know). I can probably process large amounts (weeks or months of data) without difficulty.

excerpts.author: definitelynotcharles7176
excerpts.content:
1. Download and run this geth node thingy

https://geth.ethereum.org/downloads/

Once this is installed, you have to run Geth at the command line. You'll wantt to use some special commands: light mode (so you don't have to download the whole blockchain thingy), RPC port, and a large cache helps.

`geth --rpc --rpcapi eth,net,web3,personal --cache=4420 --syncmode light  --rpcport 8545 --rpcaddr 127.0.0.1 --rpccorsdomain "*"`

excerpts.author: definitelynotcharles7176
excerpts.content:
2. Download this actually excellent Python package (has a few regular Python dependency jankiness) 

https://github.com/blockchain-etl/ethereum-etl

Run this command to use ethereum-etl

`ethereumetl export_blocks_and_transactions --start-block 11967245 --end-block 11967745 --blocks-output blocks.csv --transactions-output transactions.csv --provider-uri http://localhost:8545/
`
